Decomposition and abstraction: Decomposition: break a problem into smaller parts. Abstraction: hide the detail you don't need.
Representing algorithms: flowcharts and: Plan logic before coding: flowcharts (shapes and arrows) or pseudocode (code-like plain English).
Trace tables and types of error: A trace table tracks variable values step by step. Errors: syntax (broken rules), logic (wrong result), runtime (crash).
Linear search: Check each item in turn until you find it. Works on unsorted lists but is slow: O(n).
Binary search: Halve a sorted list each step, throwing away the half that can't hold the target. Fast: O(log n).
Bubble sort: Repeatedly swap neighbouring items that are out of order. Simple but slow: O(n squared).
Merge sort: Split the list in halves, then merge the sorted halves back together. Fast: O(n log n).
Sequence, selection and iteration: Sequence: statements in order. Selection: if/elif/else. Iteration: for/while loops.
Variables, constants and data types: A variable can change, a constant can't. Types: integer, float, Boolean, character, string.
Arithmetic, relational and logical opera: Arithmetic: calculations (including modulus and powers). Relational: compare values. Logical: AND, OR, NOT.
Lists and arrays (1D and 2D): An ordered collection, indexed from 0. A 2D list is a grid (row and column).
String handling: Slice, join (concatenate), search, split and change the case of strings, or convert them to and from numbers.
Subprograms: functions and procedures: Named, reusable blocks of code. A function returns a value; a procedure just does an action.
File handling: Read and write text files to keep data between runs. 'with open' closes the file for you.
Reading and writing CSV files: CSV: a text file holding a table, one row per line, values split by commas.
Input validation and authentication: Validation: is the input sensible (length, presence, range, type, pattern)? Authentication: who are you?
Defensive design and error handling: Expect misuse: validate input, authenticate users and handle errors so the program doesn't crash.
Testing: Test with normal data, boundary data (the edges) and erroneous data (invalid input).
Writing readable programs: Use good layout, indentation, comments, meaningful identifiers and white space.
Logic gates and truth tables: AND: both true. OR: at least one true. NOT: flips it. A truth table lists every input combination.
Binary numbers: Base 2: only 0s and 1s. 8 bits give 256 values (0-255). Add the place values wherever there's a 1.
Hexadecimal: Base 16 (0-9 then A-F). One hex digit = 4 bits, so it's a compact way to write binary.
Two's complement, binary addition, shift: Two's complement stores negatives (8 bits: -128 to 127). A left shift doubles, a right shift halves. Overflow: result too big for the bits.
Units of data storage: Bit, byte (8 bits), kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte: each about 1000 times the last.
Character encoding (ASCII and Unicode): Every character is stored as a number. ASCII: basic English. Unicode: every written language.
Representing images: A bitmap is a grid of pixels. More colour depth = more colours but a bigger file. Resolution = number of pixels.
Representing sound: Sample the sound wave at regular intervals. A higher sample rate and bit depth = better quality, bigger file.
Data compression: Lossless: the original can be rebuilt perfectly. Lossy: some data is discarded to save more space.
The CPU and the fetch-decode-execute cyc: The CPU fetches, decodes then executes instructions. Parts: control unit, ALU, clock, registers, buses.
CPU performance: A faster clock speed, a bigger cache and more cores all make a CPU quicker.
Primary storage: RAM and ROM: RAM: fast, volatile, holds running programs. ROM: non-volatile, holds start-up instructions (BIOS).
Secondary storage: solid state, magnetic: Permanent storage. Solid state (SSD): fast, no moving parts. Magnetic (HDD): cheap, big. Optical: CD, DVD.
Embedded systems: A computer built into a device to do one job, e.g. a washing machine controller.
System software and application software: System software runs the computer (e.g. the OS). Application software does user tasks (e.g. a browser).
Operating systems: Manages files, processes, memory, peripherals (through drivers), users and the interface.
Utility software: Maintenance tools: anti-malware, backup, compression, defragmentation and file repair.
High-level and low-level languages: High-level (Python): easy to write, needs a translator. Low-level (assembly, machine code): fast but tied to the hardware.
Translators: compilers and interpreters: Compiler: translates everything first, then runs. Interpreter: translates and runs line by line.
Integrated Development Environments (IDE: An IDE puts a code editor, a translator and a debugger in one place.
Network types: LAN and WAN: LAN: small area, one owner (e.g. a school). WAN: large area, uses third-party links (e.g. the internet).
Network topologies: bus, star and mesh: Bus: one shared cable. Star: every device connects to a central switch. Mesh: devices link to several others.
Wired and wireless connections and netwo: Wired (Ethernet): faster, more reliable. Wireless (Wi-Fi): convenient but limited range. Speed depends on bandwidth and latency.
The internet and protocols: TCP: splits data into packets. IP: addresses and routes them. HTTP: web pages. HTTPS: encrypted HTTP.
Email protocols: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP: SMTP sends email. IMAP reads it (it stays on the server). POP3 downloads it to your device.
The 4-layer TCP/IP model: Four layers: application (HTTP, SMTP, IMAP), transport (TCP), internet (IP) and link (NIC, drivers).
Common cyber security threats: Malware, phishing, brute-force attacks, denial-of-service, SQL injection and unpatched software.
Identifying and preventing vulnerabiliti: Find: penetration testing, ethical hacking. Prevent: firewalls, anti-malware, access control, patching.
Protecting digital systems and data: Anti-malware, encryption, acceptable use policies, and backup and recovery.
Relational database concepts: Data lives in tables. A primary key identifies each row; a foreign key links tables.
SQL: SELECT and WHERE: SELECT gets data from a table. WHERE filters which rows come back.
SQL: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE: INSERT adds a row. UPDATE changes rows. DELETE removes rows.
Environmental impacts of digital devices: Energy use, manufacturing, frequent upgrades and e-waste.
Personal data and the law: Data Protection Act and UK GDPR: how personal data must be handled. Computer Misuse Act: unauthorised access is illegal.
AI, machine learning and robotics: Issues: accountability, safety, algorithmic bias and legal liability.
Protecting intellectual property: Copyright (code), patents (inventions), trademarks (brands) and licensing (rules of use).
Cultural and social impacts of technolog: Privacy and surveillance, digital exclusion, and changes to how we work, learn and communicate.

The von Neumann concept and the CPU: Instructions and data share main memory. The CPU fetches, decodes and executes. Parts: control unit, ALU, registers, clock, three buses.
